title: Know-Nothings and Anti-Secret Crusaders
bigQuestion: How did fear of secret groups get turned against ordinary neighbors in the 1800s and early 1900s?

story.title: The March to the Courthouse
story.kicker: In April 1855, a fight over beer licenses in Chicago turns into a clash in the street.
paragraphs: It is April 1855 in Chicago. The city is young, muddy and growing fast. Many of its newest people came from Germany and Ireland. On the North Side, German families gather in beer halls after a long week of work. They talk, sing and drink lager, a kind of beer popular in Germany.

Chicago has a new mayor, Levi Boone. His side won the city election in March with a promise of law and order. The city raised the price of a yearly saloon license from $50 to $300. It also moved to close saloons on Sundays. For many immigrant families, Sunday was the one free day to gather.

Some saloon keepers would not pay. Police arrested them. Their cases came to court on April 21. That day, crowds gathered at the courthouse to support them. More marchers came from the North Side, crossing the Clark Street bridge. Police met them there, and the two sides clashed.

When it was over, one protester was dead and about 60 people had been arrested. People called it the Lager Beer Riot. Behind it was a larger fear. Mayor Boone had been elected with help from a secret order that distrusted Catholic immigrants. Its members were called the Know-Nothings.
story.think: How can a rule that seems to be about one thing, like beer, really be about something bigger?

lessons.title: Newcomers and Old Fears
lessons.mainIdea: In the 1840s and 1850s, many Irish and German immigrants arrived, and nativists feared them, largely because many were Catholic.
reading: In the late 1840s, a terrible famine struck Ireland. The potato crop failed year after year. Hundreds of thousands of Irish people sailed to America. At the same time, many Germans left home after failed revolutions and hard times. Most came to work, raise families and build new lives.

Most Irish immigrants and many German immigrants were Catholic. At that time, most American-born citizens were Protestant. Many Protestants distrusted the Catholic Church. Some claimed, without evidence, that Catholics would obey the pope instead of American laws.

An *immigrant* is a person who moves to a new country to live. The belief that people born in a country deserve more rights than newcomers is called *nativism*. Nativists saw immigrants as a threat to jobs, to elections and to the nation's religion.

In real life, most Irish and German Catholics were ordinary neighbors. They dug canals, built railroads, opened shops and joined churches. The fear did not come from what they did. It came from what others imagined they might do.

words.d: a person who moves to a new country to live
the belief that people born in a country deserve more rights than newcomers

look.title: Two Families on a Dock
look.text: Picture a New York dock in 1850. An Irish family steps off a crowded ship with one trunk. A few feet away, a German couple carries a small child and a bag of tools. Both families are tired and hungry. Both are looking for work and a place to live. Some people watching see new neighbors. Others see a threat.
look.prompt: What do the two families actually want? What might make an onlooker see a threat instead of a neighbor?

choices: The belief that people born in a country deserve more rights than newcomers
check.why: The reading defines nativism as the belief that people born in a country deserve more rights than newcomers.

choices: Worked, built, opened shops and joined churches
check.why: The reading says they dug canals, built railroads, opened shops and joined churches.

lessons.title: The Order of the Star Spangled Banner
lessons.mainIdea: The Know-Nothings began as a secret, oath-bound order whose members answered questions about it with the words 'I know nothing.'
reading: In 1849, a man named Charles B. Allen started a new society in New York City. He called it the Order of the Star Spangled Banner. The name honored the flag. But the order was not open to everyone. Members had to be native-born Protestant men.

The order was *oath-bound*. Members swore solemn promises to keep its business secret. It had passwords, secret handshakes and levels of membership. When outsiders asked about it, members replied, 'I know nothing.'

The newspaper editor Horace Greeley gave them a nickname: the *Know-Nothings*. The name stuck. Soon the order had lodges in many states. Its members met in secret, but they aimed to win public elections.

There is a sharp *irony* here. Irony is when something turns out the opposite of what you would expect. The Know-Nothings accused Catholics of a secret plot. Yet they were a secret society themselves, with hidden rules and oaths.

words.d: held together by solemn promises that members swear
the nickname for members of the Order of the Star Spangled Banner and the movement it led in the 1850s
when something turns out the opposite of what you would expect

look.title: An Imagined Night in 1854
look.text: A reporter stops a man leaving a hall late at night. What happens in there? the reporter asks. The man tips his hat. I know nothing, he says, and walks away. The reporter writes the answer in his notebook. By morning, half the town is repeating it.
look.prompt: Why would an answer like this make people curious and even more suspicious? How is it like the Masons' secrecy in the Morgan story?

check.q: Who started the Order of the Star Spangled Banner in 1849?
check.why: The reading says Charles B. Allen started the order in New York City in 1849.

check.q: How did the Know-Nothings get their name?
choices: Members answered questions about the order with 'I know nothing'
They refused to go to school
A judge named them in court
check.why: Members answered outsiders with 'I know nothing,' and Horace Greeley turned that into a nickname.

check.q: What is the irony the reading points out?
choices: The order was named after a song
The order started in New York
A secret group accused others of secret plots
check.why: The Know-Nothings accused Catholics of a secret plot while being a secret society themselves.

lessons.title: Know-Nothings in Power
lessons.mainIdea: In the mid-1850s the Know-Nothings, running as the American Party, won big elections, and then the movement faded fast.
reading: In November 1854, Know-Nothing candidates swept Massachusetts. Henry J. Gardner became governor. All but two members of the state *legislature*, the group that makes a state's laws, were Know-Nothings too. The older parties were shocked.
In public, the movement called itself the *American Party*. It wanted immigrants to wait many more years before they could become citizens and vote. It wanted only native-born men to hold office.

Election days could turn violent. On August 6, 1855, in Louisville, Kentucky, mobs of Know-Nothing supporters attacked German and Irish Catholic neighborhoods. About 22 people died. People called it Bloody Monday. The victims were ordinary families, blamed for a plot that did not exist.

In 1856, former president Millard Fillmore ran as the American Party's candidate. He won only one state, Maryland. Soon the movement split over slavery, and it faded away. Its members scattered into other parties within a few years.

words.d: the group of elected people who make a state's or nation's laws
the public name of the Know-Nothing movement when it ran candidates in elections

choices: Know-Nothings won the governor's office and almost the whole legislature

lessons.title: Mayor Boone's New Rules
lessons.mainIdea: In 1855 Chicago elected Levi Boone, whose nativist and temperance coalition raised saloon license fees in a way that hit immigrants hardest.
reading: On March 6, 1855, Chicago voters chose Levi Boone as mayor. His side was a *coalition*, a group of different people who join together for a shared goal. It joined nativists with the *temperance* movement. Temperance means cutting back on alcohol or banning it.

Under Boone, the city raised the yearly saloon *license* from $50 to $300. A license is official permission to do something, like run a business. These licenses had to be renewed every three months. The city also moved to close saloons on Sundays. Supporters said the rules would bring law and order.

Who paid the price? Many saloons and beer halls were run by German and Irish immigrants. Sunday was often the only day working people had free. A fee six times higher could shut down a small family business.
Critics saw the rules as a way to punish immigrants without saying so. Supporters said they only wanted safer, quieter streets. Either way, the rules fell hardest on the city's newest neighbors.

words.d: a group of different people or groups who join together for a shared goal
cutting back on alcohol or banning it
official permission to do something, such as run a business

choices: Cutting back on alcohol or banning it

check.why: Under Boone, the yearly fee rose from $50 to $300, six times higher.

choices: Immigrants could not vote at all

check.why: The reading says many saloons and beer halls were run by German and Irish immigrants.

lessons.title: The Lager Beer Riot
lessons.mainIdea: On April 21, 1855, a protest over the license rules became a clash with police in which one man died and about 60 people were arrested.
reading: Some saloon keepers would not pay the new fee. Police arrested them. Their cases came before a judge on April 21, 1855. Their friends and neighbors decided to show support. They planned a *protest*, a public action to show that people disagree.

Crowds gathered at the courthouse. Then more marchers came from the North Side, where many Germans lived. They crossed the Clark Street bridge toward the courthouse. Police were waiting. The two sides clashed, and shots were fired.

When it ended, one protester was dead. About 60 people were arrested. The event is called the Lager Beer Riot. A *riot* is a violent disturbance by a crowd. Lager was the German-style beer served in many beer halls.

Boone served only one year as mayor. In the next election, in 1856, Chicago voters chose a different leader, and the Know-Nothings lost power in the city. Immigrant voters had shown they would stand up for their rights.

words.d: a public action to show that people disagree with something
a violent disturbance by a crowd

look.title: Two Imagined Headlines

look.prompt: What does each headline want readers to feel? What facts would you check before trusting either one?

check.why: Marchers from the North Side crossed the Clark Street bridge, and police met them there.

check.q: What is a riot?
choices: A violent disturbance by a crowd
check.why: The reading defines a riot as a violent disturbance by a crowd.

check.q: What happened after Boone's one year as mayor?
choices: He moved the city council to Wisconsin

check.why: In the 1856 election Chicago chose a different leader, and the Know-Nothings lost power in the city.

lessons.title: Lincoln's Private Letter
lessons.mainIdea: In 1855 Abraham Lincoln of Illinois wrote privately that he was not a Know-Nothing and that their ideas broke the promise of the Declaration of Independence.
reading: In August 1855, Abraham Lincoln was a lawyer in Springfield, Illinois. He was not yet famous across the nation. On August 24, he wrote a long letter to his close friend Joshua Speed in Kentucky. In it, he said plainly that he was not a Know-Nothing.

Lincoln explained why. He had long said that slavery was wrong. He asked how a person who hated the oppression of Black people could support treating other groups as lesser people. To him, the two kinds of unfairness were connected.

He also imagined how the Know-Nothings would change the *Declaration of Independence*. It says all men are created equal. Lincoln warned that they would add exceptions: Black people, foreigners and Catholics. He meant that nativism broke the nation's founding *principle*.

Lincoln kept these words in a private letter. Historians note that he avoided attacking the Know-Nothings in public. He needed their voters in the fight to stop slavery from spreading. The letter shows what he believed when he was not speaking to a crowd.

words.d: the 1776 document that announced American independence and said all men are created equal
a basic belief or rule that guides what people do

look.title: Lincoln Writes to Joshua Speed
look.text: Lincoln wrote that he was not a Know-Nothing. He asked how anyone who hated the oppression of Black Americans could favor pushing down other groups. If the Know-Nothings took control, he warned, the Declaration would say all men are created equal, except Black people, foreigners and Catholics.
look.cite: Abraham Lincoln to Joshua F. Speed, August 24, 1855, in The Collected Works of Abraham Lincoln, ed. Roy P. Basler, vol. 2 (1953), pp. 320-323 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Which two kinds of unfairness does Lincoln connect? Why might he say this in a private letter instead of a speech?

check.why: Lincoln wrote to his close friend Joshua Speed on August 24, 1855.

check.why: Lincoln warned they would add exceptions to the Declaration's promise that all men are created equal.

check.q: Why did Lincoln avoid attacking the Know-Nothings in public, according to historians?
choices: He needed their voters in the fight to stop slavery from spreading

check.why: Historians note he needed Know-Nothing voters in the fight against the spread of slavery.

lessons.title: Jonathan Blanchard of Wheaton
lessons.mainIdea: Jonathan Blanchard, the first president of Wheaton College, spent decades arguing that every kind of secret society was wrong.
reading: Jonathan Blanchard was a minister, a teacher and an *abolitionist*, a person who worked to end slavery. Before coming to Wheaton, he led Knox College in Galesburg, Illinois. In 1860 he became the first president of Wheaton College, west of Chicago.

Blanchard believed secret societies did harm. He opposed the Masons, the Odd Fellows and every other *secret order*. His reasons were religious and political. He believed Christians should not swear secret oaths. He also believed a free country needed open, public dealing.
Blanchard was different from the Know-Nothings. They targeted Catholic immigrants. He aimed at all secret lodges, whatever their members' faith or birthplace. His fight was against secrecy itself.

Lodge members strongly disagreed with him. They said their orders raised money for widows, cared for the sick and taught good character. They saw Blanchard as attacking good neighbors. You can weigh both views.

words.d: a person who worked to end slavery
a society whose members promise to keep its ceremonies or business private

look.title: An Imagined Talk at a Church Supper
look.text: At a church supper in 1870, a Wheaton student says: My teacher says secret oaths have no place in a free country. An older farmer answers: My lodge paid for my brother's funeral when nobody else would help. Both are sure they are right.
look.prompt: What does each speaker value? Which view does Blanchard hold, and what would a lodge member say back to him?

check.q: Which college did Blanchard lead as its first president in 1860?
check.why: Blanchard became Wheaton College's first president in 1860, after leading Knox College.

check.q: How was Blanchard different from the Know-Nothings?
choices: He opposed all secret lodges, not one faith or group of immigrants
He wanted to join the Masons
check.why: The Know-Nothings targeted Catholic immigrants, while Blanchard opposed every secret lodge.

check.q: What did lodge members say in their own defense?
choices: They helped widows, cared for the sick and taught good character
check.why: The reading says members pointed to their help for widows and the sick and their lessons in character.

lessons.title: The Christian Cynosure
lessons.mainIdea: From 1868, Blanchard's National Christian Association in Chicago published the Christian Cynosure to campaign against secret societies.
reading: In 1868, Blanchard helped found the National Christian Association. Its headquarters were in Chicago. Its goal was to warn Americans against secret societies of every kind. A *campaign* like this is an organized effort to reach a goal over time.

The association published a newspaper called the Christian Cynosure, and Blanchard edited it. A *cynosure* is a guiding light, like the star that sailors steer by. For decades, the paper printed arguments, letters and reports against lodges.

The association also kept the Morgan story alive. In 1882 it paid for the Morgan Monument in Batavia, New York. More than fifty years after Morgan vanished, the monument named Masons as his killers, a claim no court had proved.

All this made Illinois a center of the movement against secret societies. Blanchard's papers and the association's records are kept today in the Wheaton College Archives. Students and researchers can still study them.

words.d: an organized effort to reach a goal over time
a guiding light, like the star sailors steer by; also something everyone looks to

look.title: Imagining One Stack of Papers
look.text: Picture a stack of the Christian Cynosure on a table in Chicago. One page retells the Morgan case from 1826. Another prints a letter from a man explaining why he left his lodge. A third asks readers to help pay for a monument in Batavia.
look.prompt: How could one newspaper keep a fifty-year-old story alive? What would you want to check before trusting one of its reports?

check.q: Where was the National Christian Association based?
check.why: The reading says the association's headquarters were in Chicago.

check.q: What does cynosure mean?
choices: A guiding light, like the star sailors steer by
check.why: A cynosure is a guiding light, like the star sailors steer by. The paper hoped to guide its readers.

check.q: How did the association keep the Morgan story alive?
choices: It closed the lodges in Vermont
It paid for the 1882 Morgan Monument
check.why: The National Christian Association paid for the Morgan Monument in Batavia in 1882.

lessons.title: The Knights of Columbus
lessons.mainIdea: The Knights of Columbus began in 1882 as a Catholic fraternal order that helped families, especially widows and children.
reading: In the early 1880s, Father Michael J. McGivney was an assistant pastor at St. Mary's Church in New Haven, Connecticut. He saw families fall into poverty when a working father died. He wanted to help.

In October 1881, he and a group of Catholic men formed a new society. On March 29, 1882, the Connecticut legislature granted it a charter. They named it the Knights of Columbus. It was a *fraternal order*, a brotherhood whose members help one another. It also offered life *insurance*, so a family would get money if the father died.

The Catholic Church did not allow Catholics to join the Masons. Many other lodges had a Protestant feel. The Knights gave Catholic men a lodge of their own, with ceremonies, charity and friendship. The order spread fast. Chicago Council No. 182, the first in Illinois, began in 1896.

Like other lodges, the Knights had private ceremonies. That privacy made them a target. Some people who already feared Catholics imagined the Knights were hiding a plot. The next lesson shows how that fear was used.

words.d: a brotherhood whose members help one another
a plan that pays money to a person or family after a loss, such as a death

look.title: A Kitchen in New Haven
look.text: Picture a New Haven kitchen in 1882. A mother sits at the table with three children. Her husband worked in a factory, and he died last month. In 1882 there is little help from the government. A letter arrives from the Knights with money from his insurance.
look.prompt: How would that money change this family's future? Why might Catholic men want to join an order like this?

check.why: Father Michael J. McGivney of St. Mary's Church in New Haven founded the Knights.

check.q: What is a fraternal order?
choices: A brotherhood whose members help one another
check.why: The reading defines a fraternal order as a brotherhood whose members help one another.

check.why: McGivney saw families fall into poverty when a father died, so the Knights offered insurance.

lessons.title: A Fake Oath Before Congress
lessons.mainIdea: A forged Knights of Columbus oath was printed in the Congressional Record in 1913 only as evidence, and a House committee condemned it as false.
reading: In 1912, Eugene Bonniwell ran for Congress in Pennsylvania and lost to Thomas Butler. Bonniwell challenged the result. His papers pointed to a false document that had been spread during the race.
That document was a *forgery*, a fake made to look real. It claimed to be the secret oath of the Knights of Columbus. It falsely said members swore to harm Protestants. No such oath was real.

A House committee studied the case. Its report was printed in the *Congressional Record*, the official record of what happens in Congress, on February 15, 1913. The fake oath was printed there too, but only as an *exhibit*, a piece of evidence in the case.

The committee did not stop there. It said it could not condemn the fake oath strongly enough. It called the document *libel*, false writing that harms someone's good name. Congress had named the oath a fake.

words.d: a fake made to look real
the official record of what is said and done in Congress
a document or object shown as evidence in a case
false writing that harms someone's good name

look.title: What the Committee Said
look.text: The committee wrote that it could not condemn too strongly the printing of the false and libelous article, which was the spurious Knights of Columbus oath.
look.cite: House Committee on Elections No. 1, report on Bonniwell v. Butler, Congressional Record, February 15, 1913, p. 3215 and following (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Which words does the committee use to describe the oath? The word spurious means fake. What does the committee's choice of words tell you?

check.q: What is a forgery?
choices: A fake made to look real
check.why: A forgery is a fake made to look real, like the false Knights of Columbus oath.

check.q: Why was the fake oath printed in the Congressional Record?
choices: Only as an exhibit, a piece of evidence in an election case
Because Congress believed it was real
To honor the Knights of Columbus

check.why: The reading says the oath appeared only as an exhibit in the Bonniwell v. Butler case.

check.q: What did the House committee say about the oath?
choices: It was the true oath of the Knights
It should be taught in schools
check.why: The committee condemned the oath as false and called it libel.

lessons.title: Copied from the Record
lessons.mainIdea: Pamphlet makers reprinted the fake oath with the label 'Copied from the Congressional Record,' hiding the fact that Congress had called it false.
reading: After 1913, anti-Catholic *pamphlets*, or short printed booklets, began to reprint the fake oath. Many carried a proud label: Copied from the Congressional Record, Feb. 15, 1913. In a narrow way the label was true. The words really had appeared there.

What the label left out was the *context*, the facts around something that give it meaning. The pamphlets did not say the oath was printed as evidence of a lie. They did not say the committee condemned it. Readers were meant to think Congress stood behind it.
This is a *misleading* use of a source. Each word on the label may be true, but the reader walks away with a false idea. Even today, people quote real documents out of context to spread fear.

Think back over this unit. Morgan's disappearance made neighbors suspect every Mason. The Know-Nothings made neighbors suspect every Catholic immigrant. The fake oath did the same to Catholic Knights. Each time, fear of a secret group landed on real people who had done nothing wrong.

words.d: short printed booklets, often meant to persuade people
the facts around something that give it meaning
giving a false idea, even when some of the words are true

look.title: Reading a Pamphlet Closely
look.text: A pamphlet printed after 1913 has big letters across the top: Copied from the Congressional Record, Feb. 15, 1913. Below them is the fake oath. Nowhere does the pamphlet say that a House committee called the oath false and libelous in that same report.
look.prompt: What is true about the label? What does it hide? Write one sentence that would give readers the missing context.

check.q: What is context?
choices: The facts around something that give it meaning
check.why: The reading defines context as the facts around something that give it meaning.

check.q: Why was the label 'Copied from the Congressional Record' misleading?

check.why: The words did appear in the Record, but the label hid that the committee called the oath false.

check.q: What pattern does the reading find across the unit?
